interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: How do Self-Supervised Remote Sensing Vision Models Transfer to Downstream Tasks?
papers.authors: Julia Romero , Qin Lv , Morteza Karimzadeh
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
papers.abstract: Self-supervised geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) learn transferable representations from remote sensing data, but their downstream behavior is difficult to characterize. We study six representative GeoFMs spanning joint-embedding, reconstruction, and multimodal pretraining families, and evaluate transfer across classification, regression, and segmentation benchmarks under different label availability and downstream pipelines. We find that model rankings change across tasks and adaptation settings. Layerwise probing shows that, in most cases, task-relevant information is more accessible in intermediate transformer blocks compared to final-layer embeddings, and that GeoFMs exhibit distinct depthwise profiles. In segmentation case studies on PASTIS and Sen1Floods11, downstream adaptation settings such as decoder design and fine-tuning can be as impactful as the choice of GeoFM, and standard dense-prediction heads may be poorly aligned with how GeoFMs organize information over depth. Finally, CKA analysis on case studies shows that fine-tuning does not rewrite GeoFMs uniformly across depth, and the strongest changes are localized to the first linear layer of the MLP in ViT blocks. These results help explain why GeoFM rankings shift across benchmarks and motivate more representation-aware evaluation and adaptation strategies.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly studies self-supervised remote sensing models, which are relevant to astronomical image analysis and transfer learning.
papers.Short digest: This paper investigates how self-supervised geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) transfer to downstream tasks like classification and segmentation. It finds that model rankings change across tasks, and that intermediate transformer blocks often contain more task-relevant information than final layers. This matters for astronomy because similar self-supervised models could be applied to JWST or survey data for source classification or anomaly detection. The paper suggests that decoder design and fine-tuning can be as important as model choice, which is a practical insight for adapting such models to astronomical images. A limitation is that the study uses remote sensing data, not astronomical images, so transferability needs verification.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for layerwise probing results showing which blocks are most informative for different tasks.
Check the segmentation case studies on PASTIS and Sen1Floods11 for decoder design comparisons.
Examine CKA analysis to understand how fine-tuning changes model representations.

papers.title: ADORE: Iterative Query Expansion with Retrieval-Grounded Relevance Feedback
papers.authors: Amin Bigdeli , Negar Arabzadeh , Radin Hamidi Rad , Sajad Ebrahimi , Charles L. A. Clarke , Ebrahim Bagheri
papers.abstract: LLM-based query expansion improves retrieval by enriching the original query with additional context. Yet most methods remain generation-driven, producing plausible pseudo-documents or expansions without checking how the target corpus responds. This can introduce retrieval drift, amplify misleading vocabulary, or miss terms that distinguish relevant from non-relevant documents. We argue that effective expansion requires retrieval-grounded feedback, not just single-pass generation or unverified iteration. We introduce ADORE (ADapt, Observe, Relevance Evaluate), an iterative framework that turns retrieval outcomes into feedback for the next expansion. At each round, an LLM generates pseudo-passages, a retriever exposes the corpus response, and a relevance assessor evaluates retrieved documents against the original query. These judgments identify what to reinforce, what remains undercovered, and what to suppress. Across TREC Deep Learning, BEIR, and BRIGHT, ADORE consistently outperforms strong query expansion baselines with notable improvements across nearly all evaluation settings, improving average nDCG@10 by 24.5% over BM25 and 3.6% over the strongest prior query expansion method on BEIR, and by 122.9% over BM25 and 9.2% over the best query expansion baseline on BRIGHT. Our code and data are publicly available.
papers.Reasons for match: Retrieval-augmented generation with iterative query expansion, directly applicable to literature review and data discovery in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem of query expansion in retrieval-augmented generation, where generated expansions can cause retrieval drift. It introduces ADORE, an iterative framework that uses retrieval outcomes as feedback to refine queries. This matters for astronomy because it can improve literature search or data discovery from large archives like ADS or MAST. The method could be used to build a research agent that iteratively refines queries to find relevant papers or datasets. A limitation is that the evaluation is on general benchmarks, not astronomy-specific corpora.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the nDCG@10 improvements on BEIR and BRIGHT to assess robustness.
Look for the relevance assessor design and how it evaluates retrieved documents.
Examine the iterative process to see if it can be adapted to multi-turn scientific discovery workflows.

papers.title: Decoupled Mixture-of-Experts for Parametric Knowledge Injection
papers.authors: Baoqing Yue , Weihang Su , Qingyao Ai , Yichen Tang , Changyue Wang , Jiacheng Kang , Jingtao Zhan , Yiqun Liu
papers.abstract: Knowledge injection aims to equip large language models (LLMs) with external, domain-specific, or time-sensitive knowledge. Existing approaches typically face a trade-off between flexibility and integration: retrieval-augmented generation keeps knowledge outside the model but only provides prompt-level augmentation, whereas post-training based methods encode new knowledge into shared parameters but may introduce catastrophic forgetting, knowledge conflict, and costly updates. In this paper, we propose Decoupled Mixture-of-Experts (DMoE), a modular architecture for parametric knowledge injection that decouples both experts and the router from the base model. DMoE converts external knowledge corpora into independently updatable expert modules and uses a lightweight uncertainty-aware router to activate relevant experts only when the base model lacks sufficient knowledge during generation. To support efficient auto-regressive inference, DMoE attaches experts only to the final-layer feed-forward network, preserving KV-cache reuse while enabling parameter-level knowledge augmentation. Experiments on knowledge-intensive benchmarks show that DMoE consistently improves answer quality over retrieval and adapter-based baselines.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses knowledge injection for LLMs via a modular expert architecture, which is relevant for building domain-specific scientific assistants for astronomy.
papers.Short digest: The paper tackles the problem of injecting external, domain-specific knowledge into large language models without catastrophic forgetting or costly retraining. It proposes Decoupled Mixture-of-Experts (DMoE), a modular architecture where external knowledge is stored in independently updatable expert modules, and a lightweight router activates relevant experts only when the base model lacks knowledge. This is relevant for astronomy because it could allow an LLM to incorporate specialized knowledge from JWST data analysis papers, catalogs, or simulation results without retraining the entire model. A concrete workflow would be using DMoE to augment a general-purpose LLM with expert modules for high-redshift galaxy SED fitting or AGN classification, enabling it to answer domain-specific queries accurately. A key caveat is that the method requires converting knowledge corpora into expert modules, which may need careful curation and preprocessing of astronomical literature or datasets.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the expert modules are designed to handle structured astronomical data (e.g., catalogs, spectra) or only text corpora.
Look for details on the uncertainty-aware router mechanism and whether it can be adapted to multi-modal inputs (images + spectra).
Examine the computational overhead of adding multiple expert modules and whether inference latency is acceptable for interactive use.

papers.title: From Chatbot to Digital Colleague: The Paradigm Shift Toward Persistent Autonomous AI
papers.authors: Yongheng Zhang , Ziang Liu , Jiaxuan Zhu , Shuai Wang , Xiangqi Chen , Haojing Huang , Jiayi Kuang , Siyu Chen , Ao Shen , Hao Wu , Qiufeng Wang , Qian-Wen Zhang , Junnan Dong , Wenhao Jiang , Ying Shen , Hai-Tao Zheng , Yinghui Li , Di Yin , Xing Sun , Philip S. Yu
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are undergoing a fundamental transformation from conversational generators into integrated AI systems capable of reasoning, action, memory, and self-improvement. We conceptualize this transition as a shift from Chatbot to Digital Colleague: from conversational answers to persistent work. We organize this transition along two tightly coupled dimensions. First, at the cognitive core level, LLMs are advancing from Chatbot-era "fast thinking" systems driven by next-token prediction toward Thinking LLMs that leverage inference-time computation, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, reflection, process supervision, and reinforcement learning to support more deliberate and reliable cognition. Second, at the tool-augmented task execution level, LLMs are progressing from tool-calling Agents that invoke external resources in an ad hoc manner toward OpenClaw-style workstation systems (OpenClaw) equipped with persistent Workspaces, skills, verification loops, and governance. The "Workspace + Skill" paradigm makes episodic tool use colleague-like via state persistence, reusable procedures, task closure, and experience reuse. We examine data construction shifts from instruction-response pairs to State-Action-Observation trajectories and evaluation from static benchmarks to sandboxed, auditable, self-evolving AI ecosystems.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly discusses the evolution of LLMs from chatbots to persistent autonomous agents with reasoning, memory, and tool use, which is core to building research agents for astronomy workflows.
papers.Short digest: This paper argues that LLMs are transitioning from simple chatbots to persistent autonomous AI systems (Digital Colleagues) that can reason, act, remember, and improve themselves. The key idea is a two-part shift: (1) at the cognitive core, moving from fast next-token prediction to deliberate thinking using chain-of-thought, reflection, and reinforcement learning; (2) at the tool-use level, moving from ad-hoc tool calling to persistent Workspaces with reusable Skills, verification loops, and governance. For astronomy, this paradigm could enable an AI agent that maintains a long-term workspace for analyzing JWST data, remembers past fitting choices, reuses validated analysis pipelines, and self-corrects. A concrete workflow would be an agent that ingests a JWST NIRSpec spectrum, runs SED fitting, checks for AGN signatures, writes a summary, and stores the procedure for reuse on the next source. A key caveat is that the paper is a conceptual framework, not a ready-to-use system, so one must check whether the proposed 'Workspace + Skill' architecture has been implemented and tested on real scientific tasks.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for any implemented system or code release that demonstrates the Workspace+Skill paradigm on a concrete task.
Check whether the paper discusses evaluation metrics relevant to scientific reproducibility, such as task completion rate or error recovery, not just benchmark scores.
See if the paper addresses how the persistent memory handles domain-specific data formats (e.g., FITS files, spectra, catalogs) or if it is purely text-based.

papers.title: SANA: What Matters for QA Agents over Massive Data Lakes?
papers.authors: Austin Senna Wijaya , Jiaxiang Liu , Haonan Wang , Eugene Wu
papers.subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Databases (cs.DB)
papers.abstract: Exploratory question answering (EQA) over data lakes requires an LLM agent to discover relevant sources, analyze retrieved data, and adapt its actions based on intermediate results. End-to-end accuracy alone cannot distinguish failures in search, planning, data analysis, or the agent's Action Policy: its decisions about what to do next and when to submit an answer. We present SANA (Search Agent Navigation Ablation framework), a diagnostic ablation framework that transforms EQA tasks into runtime profiles containing gold source sequence, sanitized subquestions, and execution records. SANA uses these profiles to construct idealized search, planning, and data-analysis tools, allowing each component to be ablated; the residual gap is diagnostic evidence for policy failures. To illustrate SANA as a reusable evaluation framework, we adapted two recent EQA benchmarks, LakeQA and KramaBench, and evaluated lightweight and mid-sized agents under fixed prompts, budgets, data lakes, and runtimes. Across both benchmarks, data analysis is a consistent bottleneck while planning is less so. Search is a major limitation in LakeQA's large data-lake setting, but less so for the smaller-scale KramaBench. SANA thus deconstructs end-to-end task accuracies into a diagnosis of where data-lake agents fail, and allows for systematic comparisons of progress in search, planning, data analysis, and agent design.
papers.Reasons for match: LLM agent framework for question answering over data lakes, relevant to scientific data discovery and analysis.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem of diagnosing failures in LLM agents for exploratory question answering over data lakes. It introduces SANA, a diagnostic ablation framework that identifies bottlenecks in search, planning, and data analysis. This matters for astronomy because similar agents could be used to query large astronomical catalogs or literature. The paper shows that data analysis is a consistent bottleneck, which is a key insight for building astronomy-specific research agents. A limitation is that the benchmarks are not astronomy-specific, so the findings may not directly transfer.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the ablation results showing which component (search, planning, data analysis) is the main bottleneck.
Check the benchmark details to see if they involve scientific or tabular data similar to astronomical catalogs.
Examine the agent design and whether it can be adapted to multi-wavelength or multi-survey data.
